The locator 'Sutrasthana — rasayana chapter' names a chapter that does not exist. Charaka's rasayana material is Chikitsasthana I (Kaviratna pp. ~1015-1065, containing Brahmya Rasayana, Chyavanaprasha, the Amalaka/Haritaki/Triphala/Pippali/Shilajatu rasayanas). Sutrasthana has no rasayana chapter. The real Ashwagandha passage is in a different sthana and a different chapter from the one cited.

In the actual rasayana chapter, Ashwagandha appears ONLY as a modern substitute for the unidentifiable classical drug 'Meda' — e.g. '(Meda) which being unobtainable, Agwagandha or Physalis flexuosa is used as a substitute' (Brahmya Rasayana, p. 1020) and the same formula in Chyavanaprasha (p. 1024). That is the translator's/commentator's interpolation, not Charaka's text. Of 28 occurrences of Ashwagandha across the whole translation, the large majority are this Meda-substitute note.

The row's energetics values (Warm; Bitter, Astringent, Sweet) come from the later nighantu tradition, not from Charaka. The cited work is silent on both. Under the founder ruling, this row currently has no valid pre-1900 support for its temperature or taste.
Orthography flag: the OCR renders Kaviratna's transliteration 'Açwagandhâ' variously as 'Afwagandha' and 'Agwagandha' (ç misread as f/g). Quoted as it stands in the scan; the printed form uses ç.
The secondary_citation is a 2011 PubMed paper (PMID 22754076), which is explicitly forbidden as energetics support.

results.supportsWhat: Supports taste 'Sweet' (味甘), supports 'Cold' for the raw/dried root (寒), and supports the marrow-filling and flesh-building framing (填骨髓，長肌肉) behind the energetics summary. concerns: The row's headline temperature and taste match a DIFFERENT pre-1900 work exactly, and that work is not the one cited. Bencao Gangmu (1596) 卷十六, entry 熟地黃, reads: 氣味甘微苦微溫無毒 — sweet, slightly bitter, slightly warm, non-toxic. That is verbatim the row's taste 'Sweet, Slightly bitter' and its temperature 'Warm (prepared)'. Verified via https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷16&action=raw. Note the SKQS text uses the variant 黄, so a grep on 黃 finds nothing — that trap could easily make an auditor call this source silent.

The same Bencao Gangmu juan also carries the raw-versus-prepared distinction the row depends on, under 乾地黃修治: 藏器曰…蒸乾即溫補生乾即平宣 (steam-dried is warming and tonifying; sun-dried is neutral and dispersing), and 時珍曰…鮮用則寒乾用則涼. The correct citation for this row is Bencao Gangmu 卷十六, not the Shennong Bencao Jing.

One textual note: the Sun Xingyan text at this point reads 通利水殺 with an editorial gloss 「《御覽》，此下有道字」. The received reading is 通利水穀 ("freely moves water and grain"); 殺 is a transmission corruption. I have given the emended reading in the excerpt and am flagging it rather than passing it silently.

No recension is named. The Shennong Bencao Jing exists only through later reconstructions; a citation to it that does not name one (Sun Xingyan 1799, Mori Tateyuki, Gu Guanguang, etc.) is not verifiable in principle. Note also that the Sun Xingyan text heads the entry 鞠華, an older orthography — searching for 菊花 in that recension will not find it, which is a plausible route by which someone could have concluded the entry was unfindable, or never looked.

The claim "listed among the superior / upper-grade herbs" IS correct — I verified it by position (between 菖蒲 and 人參, both upper grade) and independently in the Bencao Gangmu, where Li Shizhen writes 「神農列之上品」. That part of the citation checks out.

WORLDVIEW FILTER: the second half of the Shennong entry is 「久服，利血氣，輕身、耐老、延年」 — with prolonged use it lightens the body, resists ageing, and extends years. That is precisely the life-extension framing on the do-not-surface list, and I have deliberately excluded it from the supporting excerpt. The first half (indications) is clean and publishable. Roughly half the entry is unusable for this brand, and the Bencao Gangmu's 發明 commentary on chrysanthemum is heavier still — it runs into 得金水之精英, immortality anecdotes (康風子、朱孺子皆以服菊花成仙), and 神仙食也. concerns: FORBIDDEN SOURCE FOR ENERGETICS. Stuart (1911) is named on the founder's exclusion list and is post-1900. The row's Cold temperature and Sweet taste have no admissible support.

TASTE ACTIVELY CONTRADICTED, EVEN SETTING THE DATE RULE ASIDE. The row records taste 'Sweet'. The only organoleptic word in Stuart's entry is ASTRINGENT. This is the Ginkgo failure mode running in reverse: there, a row claimed 'astringent and warming' from a source that said neutral; here a row claims 'sweet' from a source that says astringent.

THE CITATION IS A COMPOSITE OF TWO DIFFERENT WORKS AND ONE OF THEM DOES NOT CONTAIN THIS HERB. The title field names Stuart 1911. I downloaded and searched the King's index: there is NO Lonicera entry and no Chinese honeysuckle entry. The only 'Honeysuckle' in King's is Diervilla, Bush Honeysuckle — a different genus. The URL a reader would click resolves to a work that has nothing to say about this plant.

METAPHYSICAL FRAMING PRESENT AND WITHHELD. Stuart's entry also states that 'Prolonged use is said to increase vitality and to lengthen life' (p. 247), rendering the 久服…延年 formula. No pre-1900 source was consulted for this herb at all, though 忍冬 has a substantial Bencao Gangmu (1596) entry that would be admissible. Note also that 忍冬 appears in the Shennong Bencao Jing ONLY as an alias of 麥門冬 (Wu Pu's gloss, line 350) — it is not a Shennong drug in its own right, so no one should later 'fix' this row by pointing it at the Shennong classic.

The row's 'tonic' identity leans on exactly the life-extension formula this brand cannot publish; strip it and the entry supports little more than 'sweet, neutral, for wasting and breathlessness'.
MOISTURE UNSUPPORTED. 'Moist' and the entire 'bathes a dry, spent Lung and Stomach' summary have no basis in the cited entry. 胃絡脈絕 concerns the stomach network vessels, not fluids.

Note the direction of the discrepancy is interesting and worth the founder's attention: SNBCJ does NOT flag Ban Xia as 有毒 in the entry proper even though it is a lower-class drug, yet the drug-relations appendix names 半夏毒 outright. Does NOT support: the Spleen-strengthening claim — the character 脾 appears nowhere in the entry, and 'firms and strengthens a boggy, deficient Spleen' is the row's central energetics claim; does NOT support 'bland' as a taste (the source gives 甘 only, not 淡); does NOT support any of the four commercial grades named in part_used.

Fu Ling Pi / Chi Fu Ling / Bai Fu Ling are post-classical commercial distinctions and cannot rest on this citation.

The citation title's phrase 'listed among the superior, long-life tonic herbs' is half right and half unpublishable. The 上經 (superior class) placement is correct and verified. But 'long-life' points at 久服，安魂、養神，不飢、延年 — the life-extension framing the brand cannot surface. I have deliberately excluded that clause from the excerpt; the row's calming claim does not need it.

The parenthetical （《御覽》作疝氣） inside the quoted line is Sun Xingyan's editorial variant-reading note (Taiping Yulan reads 疝氣 for 逆氣), not part of the Han-era text. Retained for verbatim fidelity, flagged rather than silently stripped.

The Wikisource transcription has DROPPED the ==茯苓== section heading; the entry runs on headerless after the 柏實 philological note. Anyone re-checking by searching for the heading will wrongly conclude the entry is absent.

results.supportsWhat: SUPPORTS temperature (溫, warm) exactly, and the bitter half of the taste (苦). Supports the damp claim via 風寒濕痹, digestion via 消食, and — a genuinely good match — the row's 'shores up a weak, spontaneously sweating protective exterior' via 止汗 (stops sweating). Does NOT support: the SWEET taste, which the row uses to carry its whole tonic mechanism ('the sweetness tonifies and nourishes the Spleen qi'); the source gives 苦 only. Does NOT support the Spleen (脾 does not occur). Does NOT support the identification of the drug as Atractylodes macrocephala specifically.
concerns: Species resolution is the serious problem. The cited text has ONE undifferentiated 術. The Bai Zhu / Cang Zhu split (A. macrocephala vs A. lancea) is not in this source at all — it postdates it by centuries. Attributing a monograph on A. macrocephala to this entry claims a precision the source does not have.

results.supportsWhat: Supports: part used (rhizome and roots); the exact taste triad — the U.S.P. 'taste sweetish, bitter and pungent' independently underwrites bitter + pungent + the faint initial sweetness; the vermifuge indication, especially in children; the narrow toxic margin and its symptom picture; and the row's 'always swept out afterward by a cathartic', which is King's own dosing protocol. It does NOT state a temperature, does NOT state a moisture, and does NOT say the root is gathered in autumn.
concerns: Temperature 'Cool' has no support. King's grades no temperature for Spigelia anywhere in the entry. Same for moisture 'Dry'.

AUTUMN HARVEST IS NOT IN THE SOURCE. The row says 'Dried root and rhizome, gathered in autumn.' I grepped the whole entry: the word autumn does not occur. What King's actually says about timing is the opposite kind of statement — 'Age impairs the virtues of pinkroot.' The autumn detail appears to have been carried over from a neighbouring row (King's does specify autumn for Cypripedium and for Phytolacca, both in this same batch).

SPECIES MISMATCH ON THE TOXICITY CLAIM. The row says 'The fresh root is more acrid and is considered unsafe.' The only 'fresh plant is very poisonous' sentence in this entry belongs to Spigelia ANTHELMIA (Demerara pinkroot), a different species treated under Related Species, of which King's says it 'possesses decided narcotic qualities.' King's makes no fresh-vs-dried safety statement about S. marilandica. This is the same class of error as the withdrawn Ginkgo citation: a true sentence from the page, attached to the wrong plant.

The row attributes the acrid/nauseous taste to 'the narcotic alkaloid.' King's is more equivocal: Stabler located the activity in 'a bitter, acrid principle… non-volatile, neutral', and Dudley's volatile alkaloid spigeline came later (1879); King's also relays Maisch's suspicion that spigelia's reputed virtues may in fact belong to adulterant Phlox Carolina. Confident single-constituent attribution overstates the source.

Adulteration warning present in the source and absent from the row: 'Often the roots of other plants, particularly those of Phlox Carolina, Linné… will be found mixed with those of spigelia.' For a narrow-margin vermifuge this is safety-relevant.

results.supportsWhat: Supports, very fully: root as the principal drug; autumn harvest ('the latter weeks of autumn'); the berry's older rheumatism use, in gin, exactly as the row describes; poke sallet as spring shoots eaten as a vegetable; the alterative/lymphatic/glandular indication set including mastitis, tonsillitis and scrofulous swellings; and the narrow toxic margin (emeto-catharsis, spinal-cord paralysis, respiratory death). concerns: THE STORED TASTE CONTRADICTS THE SOURCE. The row says 'Bitter and acrid (pungent)… with an astringent edge.' Acrid is confirmed; SWEETISH is what the source pairs it with, and bitter is not the word used. The row has dropped the sweetish note and substituted bitter.

THE ASTRINGENT EDGE IS AFFIRMATIVELY CONTRADICTED. Frankforter's quantitative analysis, as King's reports it, states 'the absence of acetic, citric, malic, tartaric, benzoic, and salicylic acids are affirmed, likewise THE ABSENCE OF TANNIN and of chlorides.' The row grounds its astringency in tannins the cited source says are not there.

Temperature 'Cool' is not in King's. I grepped the entry for cool/cooling: zero occurrences. The row's temperature paragraph is candid that it is 'read across the modern Western tradition' — that is an accurate description of its provenance, and it means the Cool grading rests on post-1900 authors (Mills & Bone, Bartram, Wood, all in the secondary), none of which are admissible for energetics.

Latin-name divergence, benign but worth recording: King's treats the drug under Phytolacca DECANDRA Linné; the row stores Phytolacca americana. These are accepted synonyms, so this is not a species error, but the citation should say which name the 1898 text actually uses.

Preparation detail not in the source: the row says poke sallet is safe 'only after repeated changes of boiling water.' King's describes the spring shoots as eaten as a vegetable with no such instruction, and separately condemns berry pies. The repeated-water instruction is real folk practice but it is not in the cited page.
Secondary citation contributes nothing admissible — AHPA (2013), Mills & Bone (2005), Bartram and Wood are all post-1900.

The row's temperature and taste paragraphs are written in Chinese medical terms and cite their reasoning to Chinese sources — but every Chinese source on this row sits in the SECONDARY citation and is forbidden (Bensky, Chen & Chen). report:
# The citation layer of the 200-herb expansion: verdict

## 1. How bad is it

**126 of the 201 rows now have a real, verbatim, re-findable passage behind them. 75 do not.** That is 63 percent recovered, 37 percent not.

| Verdict | Rows | Share |
|---|---|---|
| EXCERPT_RECOVERED | 126 | 62.7% |
| POST1900_ONLY | 62 | 30.8% |
| SOURCE_SILENT | 9 | 4.5% |
| WRONG_SPECIES | 3 | 1.5% |
| ONLY_METAPHYSICAL_SUPPORT | 1 | 0.5% |
| **Total audited** | **201** | |

The 75 failures split into two very different problems, and the distinction matters more than the total.

**62 rows cite a source that genuinely exists and genuinely says something, but is post-1900 and therefore inadmissible for energetics.** Nobody made anything up. Grieve's *A Modern Herbal* (1931), Ellingwood (1919), and the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India are real books that were really consulted. They are simply on the forbidden list, so every temperature, moisture and taste value resting on them is ineligible on its face, before any question of what the passage says. These rows are wrong in the sense that a bank statement in the wrong currency is wrong.

**13 rows have nothing at all.** Nine where the named source is silent on the claim, three where the citation points at a different plant, one where the only support is metaphysical framing the worldview filter excludes. These are the ones in the same family as the four you already withdrew.

Notice what is not in that table: **zero WORK_DOES_NOT_EXIST verdicts.** Every book named in these 201 rows is a real book. That is genuinely reassuring and it narrows what went wrong.

One number that is not reassuring. 1,078 concerns were raised across 201 rows, an average of 5.4 per row. Rows are not failing on one technicality each. They are failing on several things at once: wrong source, wrong field, missing locator, dead URL, unsupported taste, unsupported temperature, all on the same record.

**The blunt version.** Sixty-three percent recovery sounds like a passing grade and it is not one. Read the recovered excerpts and a second problem shows through: they overwhelmingly support the *indications* and the *taste*, and are silent on *temperature and moisture*. King's American Dispensatory is superb on taste, part used and action, and categorically unusable on hot and cold, because the Eclectic tradition does not think in those terms. Charaka assigns functional class and never assigns rasa or virya. So a row can be counted EXCERPT_RECOVERED and still have an unsourced temperature field. The true figure for "energetics properly sourced" is lower than 126 and I cannot tell you what it is from the verdict counts alone. That is the single most important caveat in this report.

## 2. The unsupportable citations, named

These have to come out the way the earlier four did.

I have to be straight about the limits of what I can name. **The audit returned 13 hard failures. The detailed verdicts in front of me cover about 29 of the 201 rows, and only 2 of the 13 appear in them.** The other 11 are counted but not itemised in the material I was given. Anyone reading this should ask for the full itemisation before treating the withdrawal list as complete. What follows is the part I can vouch for.

**H120 Spikenard / Jatamansi (*Nardostachys jatamansi*), WRONG_SPECIES.** The row cites Grieve for an entry that distinguishes Indian or true nard from American Spikenard. Grieve contains no such entry and draws no such distinction. What Grieve actually has is *Aralia racemosa*, American Spikenard, a plant in a different family, described as "taste mucilaginous, pungent and slightly acrid" and "stimulant, diaphoretic, alterative". The row stores cool, bitter and settling. The citation points at something close to the opposite plant.

The mechanism is worth writing down because it will recur. Grieve's *Aralia racemosa* entry lists "Indian Spikenard" among its synonyms. Anyone searching Grieve for "Indian Spikenard" lands on the wrong plant and comes away with a citation that sounds exactly right. This row has no admissible source at any level: every work in its secondary citation is post-1900 too, and two of them are individually on the forbidden list.

**H126 Haritaki (*Terminalia chebula*), SOURCE_SILENT.** The row cites Grieve under the heading "Myrobalans (Chebulic)". A sweep of Grieve's complete common-name index, all 26 letter pages, 979 entries, returned zero occurrences of "myrobalan", "chebulic" or "Terminalia". Under "My-" the only entry in the entire work is Myrrh. This is the same shape as the withdrawn Maitake citation: a real and respectable book, a plausible-sounding heading, and the heading is not in the book. I would treat this citation as fabricated unless someone produces a page image from a print edition. The row's five stored tastes and its temperature currently rest on nothing: its secondary citation leads with the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India and Bensky, both forbidden.

Two more that are filed as POST1900_ONLY but belong on the withdrawal list for a different reason.

**H102 Hibiscus (*Hibiscus sabdariffa*).** The citation object is internally incoherent. The author and year fields say Grieve, 1931. The title and locator fields say Egyptian Herbal Monograph, Egyptian Drug Authority, 2023. One database record is standing in for two unrelated works ninety-two years apart. Both are post-1900. No Hibiscus entry could be located in Grieve at all. This row has no valid energetics source of any kind and nothing was found to replace it.

**H151 Common Mallow (*Malva sylvestris*).** The stored title reads "A Modern Herbal (1898 material medica tradition, published 1931)". There is no 1898 tradition behind Grieve. That phrase has no bibliographic basis, and its only effect is to make a 1931 book look as though it satisfies the 1899-or-earlier rule. "Material medica" is also a misspelling of materia medica. This is the most suspicious string in everything I read, and it reads as provenance engineered to pass a cutoff check rather than as an honest mistake.

### One safety item, escalated on its own

**H110 Saffron** states in its energetics summary that saffron is "therapeutic in milligrams and toxic in grams". **No source anywhere on that row supports it.** Grieve's saffron entry mentions no toxicity at all. King's mentions none. This is a dose-threshold claim published with nothing behind it, on a herb where dose genuinely matters. Of the 1,078 concerns raised, this is the one with a physical consequence, and it should be resolved ahead of anything else in this report.

## 3. Did the "written to justify the value" shape recur

Yes, but in a different and in some ways more troubling form than Lion's Mane.

Lion's Mane was caught because a quoted line said exactly what the database already stored. That specific shape, an invented quotation, **did not recur.** Every quoted passage checked in this audit turned out to be real text in a real book. Where a source matched a stored value it also failed to match neighbouring values on the same row, which is what an honest read of a source looks like: Grieve gives saffron bitter, and the row also claims pungent and sweet, which Grieve does not.

What recurred instead is **reverse citation**. The value was taken from a real source, and then attributed to a different, older, more respectable-sounding source that does not contain it. The quotation is not fabricated. The provenance is.

| Row | Stored value | Where it actually comes from | What the row cites |
|---|---|---|---|
| H104 Rehmannia | "Sweet, slightly bitter", "Warm (prepared)" | *Bencao Gangmu* 卷十六, character for character | Shennong Ben Cao Jing |
| H148 Arjuna | Astringent, Cool, Dry | Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia monograph convention (kashaya rasa, shita virya, laghu-ruksha guna), matching all three including the Dry no pre-1900 source states | API named as primary, with a 2007 journal paper stored under the author "Charaka Samhita" |
| H152 Figwort | "Bitter, Pungent (slightly acrid)" | King's 1898, near-verbatim including the unusual qualifier "slightly acrid" | Grieve 1931 |

H104 is the clearest illustration. The passage is real, I read it, and the stored values reproduce it exactly. The row simply cites the wrong Chinese classic: whoever built it had the standard values in hand and attached the most famous-sounding title rather than the one that actually carries them. As the audit note puts it, that is the same authoring motion as a fabrication with a luckier landing.

H148 is the worst instance because the label is actively false. Its secondary citation carries author "Charaka Samhita", year "classical", kind "public_domain_text", and a title naming two modern pharmacology papers from 2007 and 2014. A modern journal article is sitting in your database wearing an ancient work's name and flagged as public-domain classical text. That is not a weak citation. Related, its primary citation stores the year as "ongoing", which is not a year and would defeat any automated pre-1900 check on that row. H147 Gokshura stores the year "classical" for a modern Government of India pharmacopoeia and puts "Charaka Samhita" in the author field of an API citation.

**How often.** Three unambiguous instances plus H151's engineered date claim, out of roughly 29 rows I can see in detail. I will not extrapolate that to a rate across 201, because the detail simply is not in front of me. But the mechanism is clearly systemic rather than incidental, and the right assumption is that it is present in the rows I cannot see.

## 4. The pattern in the failures

There is a clear one, and it says more than the list does.

**This is one authoring pass, and it can be bounded.** The 201 are H001 plus H101 through H300, which is the entire expansion. The original hundred carry excerpts. Nothing here suggests a corrupt database. It suggests one working session, or one person, or one prompt, that recorded *which book* a claim came from instead of *which passage*, and that habit produced every other symptom below.

**Grieve was the fallback whenever the allowed corpus ran thin.** Eight of ten rows in the first slice cite Grieve as primary on an energetics-bearing row. Look at which herbs those are and the logic is visible: saffron is dismissed by King's as near-inert, coriander gets a sentence, *Nigella* is absent from King's entirely. Grieve got reached for exactly where the Eclectic corpus ran out. The problem is that the alternative was not "no source", it was "the Indian pre-1900 corpus", which covers all three of those herbs and was apparently never opened.

**The traditions fail differently, and each failure is characteristic of its corpus.**

- *Eclectic (King's, Ellingwood).* Excellent for taste, part used, action, indication. Silent on temperature by design. Where King's is cited on an energetics row, expect the temperature field to be unsupported. White Oak's "Cool" and Juniper's "Warm" have no textual basis whatever in the cited entries.
- *Ayurvedic.* Charaka supports functional class and assigns no rasa and no virya to individual herbs. The energetic values in these rows come from later nighantus that are not cited. The authoring pass filled that gap with the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, which is forbidden, and in several rows labelled it "classical".
- *Chinese.* Small sample, but H104 cites the wrong classic for a real value, and H147 hedges a straight contradiction: the row calls the Chinese classification "slightly warm" and "pungent and mildly bitter", while the Shennong entry says bitter and warm outright, and the row then overrides even that with a Cool anchor sourced to a forbidden work. Two traditions disagreeing about temperature, and the citation does not disclose it.

**The citation objects are structurally decorative, and this is the root cause worth fixing before any content work.** Across every row examined: the `locator` field is a verbatim copy of the `title` field, so no row has an actual locator. The `url` points at a site root or a corpus index rather than an entry, so no row points at the passage. Author and year are stale carry-over from neighbouring records, which is how a 2023 Egyptian monograph ends up attributed to Grieve 1931. Multiple works, sometimes six, are crammed into one title string, which makes it impossible to say which work supports which claim and lets a forbidden source ride along invisibly behind an allowed one. Several title strings are truncated mid-word around 200 characters, so the lists are incomplete as stored. **Any automated check keying on author, year or kind will draw the wrong conclusion about roughly half these rows.** Filling in excerpts without fixing this would attach real quotations to wrong authors and wrong years.

**The most useful pattern is the most hopeful one.** Over and over, a clean allowed pre-1900 source that supports the row already exists, and is either uncited or demoted to secondary while the forbidden source sits in the primary slot. On H110 Saffron, King's 1898 supports the bitter taste and the emmenagogue action and is sitting in secondary behind Grieve. Primary and secondary look simply swapped. That is not an authoring judgment failure. It is a filing failure, which is cheaper to fix.

**One contradiction rather than a gap, which needs your decision and not a quiet edit.** H123 Selfheal stores temperature Cool. Culpeper (1653), an allowed source cited by that very row, grades it "moderately hot and dry, binding". Culpeper is also internally two-sided: his virtues section indicates the herb against heat while his simples list grades the substance itself as hot. That is the substance-versus-action conflation already known from the herb-verdict rebuild, and it is live here and it decides whether Cool survives. H105 Prickly Ash is stored Dry while King's describes it as a sialagogue prescribed *for* dryness. H141 Shepherd's Purse is stored Cool while King's calls it stimulating. H111 Coriander is stored Cool while both its cited works call it a stimulant, and in that case the row is right and the citation is the wrong book.

## 5. What can be loaded

**126 rows have a recovered verbatim excerpt ready to fill the gap.** That is the headline, and three qualifications go with it.

First, a recovered excerpt is not a recovered energetic. The excerpts mostly support indications, taste and part used. Temperature and moisture remain the thinnest fields on the majority of rows, including many of the 126. Loading the excerpts closes the auditability gap, which is the gap that let the four fabrications through, but it does not validate the energetics.

Second, the excerpts cannot safely be attached to citation objects whose author, year and locator fields are wrong. On current structure, a correct quotation would be filed under an incorrect attribution on a meaningful share of rows. The schema problem is upstream of the content problem and should be settled first.

Third, and this is the good news buried in the failures: the audit did not only diagnose the 62 post-1900 rows, it found named allowed replacements for a dozen of them.

| H111 Coriander | Dutt 1877 | "refrigerent", internal heat and thirst, carminative. Supplies the Cool the row needs |
| H121 Cumin | Culpeper 1653 | "heat, bind, and dry ... expel wind". Warm plus Dry plus carminative in one line |
| H125 Amalaki | Dutt 1877 | "cooling, refrigerant", "acidulous, astringent taste". Cool, Sour, Astringent |
| H128 Cardamom | Dymock 1890-93, vol. III p. 428 | "digestive, pungent, light and hot". Pungent, Warm, drying |
| H130 Kalmegh | Dymock 1890-93, vol. III pp. 46-48 | "intensely bitter", tannic acid basis for Astringent, fever use |
| H131 Neem | Dymock 1890-93, vol. I p. 323 | "bitter, tonic, and astringent". Both stored tastes in one sentence |
| H141 Shepherd's Purse | King's 1898 | "a pungent, biting taste, which is lost by drying". Also supports "fresh where possible" |
| H147 Gokshura | Dutt 1877 | "cooling", diuretic, urinary indications |

None of these has been written anywhere. They are candidates for your decision, not changes. Two carry conditions: several Culpeper passages open with astrological attribution ("Venus owns them both", "under the dominion of the Sun") and Dutt's myrobalan material opens with "life-giver" and "nectar" language, all of which the worldview filter excludes and none of which may be surfaced as supporting evidence even when the rest of the passage is used.

Note what these substitutes do not fix. Not one of them supplies a temperature for Neem, Haritaki, Kalmegh or Centaury. On several rows the honest outcome is that no source located in this audit states a temperature at all, and "Cool" is an inference rather than a quotation.

## 6. What remains unknown

Sources that could not be reached are not the same as sources that are silent, and I want to keep those apart because it would be easy to record an unverified row as disproven.

**Genuinely unresolved, in both directions.**

- **H130 Kalmegh.** I could not confirm whether a Grieve entry titled "Kariyat" exists. It is absent from botanical.com's K index and from the whole of print Volume I, but Volume II, which is where K would fall, is lending-restricted on archive.org and returned HTTP 401 on every copy. This is unverified, not absent. There is a specific trap here: the archive.org copy catalogued as the 1931 *A Modern Herbal* is Volume I only and ends at page 427. A first pass over it returns zero hits for "Kariyat" and would support a confident and entirely wrong conclusion.
- **H102 Hibiscus.** Reported as not-found rather than absent. The OCR searched renders "Althaea" zero times despite the book containing a Marsh Mallow entry, so that text layer is demonstrably lossy. Watt's *Dictionary of the Economic Products of India* (1889-93) is the most likely allowed work to carry *Hibiscus sabdariffa* and was not checked.
- **H126 Haritaki.** The conclusion rests on the botanical.com transcription, which is the standard electronic text but not the print edition. If you want belt and braces before withdrawing, a print-edition index check is the confirming step and it was not done.

**Not reachable at all.**

- **botanical.com**, the host that the largest number of these rows point at, sits behind ModSecurity and returns "Not Acceptable" or 404 to ordinary requests. A customer or reviewer trying to check any Grieve citation gets nothing, and cannot distinguish a real citation from a fabricated one. That is a verification problem independent of whether the underlying passages are sound. It is also proof that whoever wrote several of these citations did not read the entry at the address they supplied: H131 Neem's Margosa entry exists in print and is not on botanical.com under any slug, so the pointer and the content do not coexist anywhere.
- **ayush.gov.in** returned no response at all (curl exit, HTTP 000). So for H148 Arjuna I never read the API text. The verdict rests on the source class being inadmissible, not on what the monograph says.
- **Bhavaprakasha Nighantu**, named as corroboration on H147, is genuinely pre-1600 but is not on the approved allowlist and no verifiable text with a locator could be obtained.

**Not yet attempted.**

- Dymock for H112's Warm, which is the obvious next place to look and was not reached.
- Any substitute for H120 Spikenard. Dymock, Dutt and Ainslie are plausible candidates and none was opened. That row currently has no admissible source at any level and no verified replacement.
- **A bulk HTTP check on the `url` field across all 300 rows.** H001's archive.org identifier is a 404 whose metadata endpoint returns empty. It follows the plausible-looking Google-scan naming convention and does not exist, which means nobody ever opened it. That check is cheap and would find the rest of these immediately.
- Itemisation of 11 of the 13 hard failures, as noted in section 2.

**One method note worth keeping.** Two traps cost real time and will recur on the remaining work. The Siku Quanshu wikitext of *Bencao Gangmu* uses the variant character 黄 rather than 黃, so searching the standard form returns zero hits on a juan that contains the entry, which would produce a false SOURCE_SILENT. And archive.org OCR quality varies wildly between copies of the same book: Grieve Volume 1 exists both as a usable 2.0 MB text layer and as a 4.8 KB stub. Byte size should be checked and the text spot-read before any term is declared absent.

---

**Where this leaves you.** The expansion's citation layer is not fraudulent. It is unverifiable, which for a product that stakes its claim on pre-1900 sourcing is close enough to the same thing from the outside. Two rows must be withdrawn on the evidence in hand, eleven more are counted as hard failures and need naming before you can act on them, one unsourced dose-threshold claim on saffron should be dealt with today, and sixty-two rows are carrying energetics values on books your own rule forbids. Against that, twelve of those sixty-two already have a real pre-1900 passage identified and waiting, the damage is confined to a single authoring pass, and the original hundred rows are clean. The fixable thing is not the herbs. It is the habit of recording which book a claim came from instead of which passage.
